rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Test a strong temperature shift at the same gradient to probe selectivity within the crowded four-peak cluster and the late critical pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent slope refinement.

Complete the temperature screen at fixed gradient to test whether cooler conditions separate the crowded cluster and late pair. This isolates temperature-driven selectivity before adjusting gradient slope.
Keep the best temperature and make the gradient shallower to improve the two unresolved pairs. The current 7.30-minute last peak provides some headroom before the 10-minute time penalty.

Use a shallower gradient to further separate the remaining critical pair, whose selectivity changed substantially between the last two runs. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the longer gradient and help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.
Slightly flatten the gradient to lift the remaining R = 1.40 pair above 1.5. Raising the starting organic fraction should preserve a last-peak time below 10 minutes, targeting the maximum CRF of 1.0.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten elution while retaining full resolution. The slightly shallower gradient may help protect the critical pair, which currently has little resolution margin.

Return to the successful starting composition and test a one-step shorter gradient. This probes whether elution can be accelerated without losing full resolution; injection 6 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Restore the successful gradient and raise temperature by one step to seek faster elution with full resolution. This tests temperature selectivity locally, since shortening the gradient or raising the starting organic fraction weakened the critical pair.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient at 30 C to rebalance the two close early pairs. The longer gradient aims to preserve their resolution while the higher starting fraction targets faster elution than injection 6.

Flatten the latest gradient by one step to improve the R = 1.30 pair, targeting full resolution with a last peak still earlier than injection 6. Monitor the other close early pair and the late R = 1.65 pair for selectivity losses.

Lower the temperature to restore late-pair selectivity while retaining the shallow gradient needed for the crowded early peaks. This tests whether the higher starting composition can deliver full resolution faster than injection 6.

With maximum-score methods secured, test a substantially higher starting composition for a shorter elution window. The critical pair may reverse order and regain separation beyond the co-elution region, though other early pairs must also be checked.
Shorten the gradient at the newly successful starting composition to reduce elution time. The minimum resolution of 1.98 provides some margin for testing a steeper gradient while retaining CRF 1.0.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek faster full separation. Watch the late R = 1.79 pair and the middle R = 1.96 pair, which are most likely to limit further acceleration.
Test one more gradient-shortening step to locate the full-resolution boundary. Injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if either marginal pair falls below R = 1.5.

Restore the last fully resolving gradient duration and raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek earlier elution. This tests a different selectivity adjustment after the 10-minute gradient weakened two pairs.

Test whether a larger temperature shift moves the nearly co-eluting middle pair past its selectivity crossover and restores separation in this shorter elution window. Injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Combine the fastest confirmed fully resolving gradient with an intermediate temperature to seek a shorter separation. Lowering the starting organic fraction relative to injection 18 should spread the crowded early peaks, while the temperature change probes a different selectivity balance.

Test an intermediate temperature with a shallower gradient to improve the crowded early peaks seen at 40 C. The higher starting organic fraction may separate the middle pair beyond its crossover while preserving a shorter elution window than injection 15.

Test a steeper gradient at 35 C to move the remaining middle pair away from its apparent selectivity crossover while shortening elution. Check whether the two earlier pairs retain R ≥ 1.5; injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction separates the middle pair beyond its crossover, using a shallower gradient to protect other pairs. The maximum CRF is already secured; this explores a potentially shorter fully resolved method.

Refine the gradient slope between the fully resolved injection 15 and the slightly too-steep injection 16 by lowering the endpoint and shortening the programmed gradient. This targets a modestly earlier last peak while testing the resolution boundary of the two limiting pairs.

Match injection 15’s successful gradient slope but end the programmed ramp after four minutes. The gradient endpoint reaches the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the previously observed 4.14-minute last peak, so full resolution should be preserved with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test the minimum programmed gradient duration while preserving the successful initial slope, then hold at 45% organic. Early-pair resolution should be retained; this final run checks whether the later peaks remain fully resolved and elute within 10 minutes, with injection 24 retained as a confirmed maximum-score method.
